To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) variable elimination is a powerful algorithm for inference in graphical models; (ii) the treewidth of a graphical model is a measure of its computational complexity; (iii) low-treewidth models can be processed efficiently; (iv) approximate inference can be linked to the variable elimination principle.

(i) the treewidth characterizes the computational complexity of inference in graphical models; (ii) the treewidth can be computed efficiently in practice; (iii) the treewidth of real-world models is low in practice; (iv) low-treewidth models can be solved efficiently in practice; and (v) low-treewidht models arise in many real-world problems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of efficient inference methods for graphical models, with the aim of making them accessible to the statistician.
the study of efficient algorithms for exact and approximate inference in probabilistic graphical models, and their implementation in software.
exact and approximate inference in probabilistic graphical models.

variable elimination, and its variants, should be the first choice for inference in graphs with low treewidth, and loopy belief propagation should be the first alternative for inference in high-treewidth graphs.
the graph structure of a graphical model is an important source of information to be exploited to design efficient algorithms for inference.
exact and approximate inference techniques based on variable elimination and treewidth are a powerful tool for inference and learning in graphical models.

the treewidth of the underlying graphical structure is the key quantity to assess the computational complexity of exact or approximate inference in graphical model, and that the treewidth can be efficiently computed for a wide range of graphs.
